topicDisplay: Hl Core Extension Global Interactions Power Places Networks; Human Development Diversity; Global Risks Resilience
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Why can a country have a high GNI per capita but a low HDI?
options: Wealth may be unevenly invested, leaving health and education indicators weak
questions.explain: Resource-rich states can have high average income yet poor schooling and life expectancy if wealth is not invested in people.

questions.q: Which best describes 'tied aid'?
options: Aid given only after a natural disaster
Aid that must be spent on goods or services from the donor country
questions.explain: Tied aid requires the recipient to purchase from the donor, reducing the aid's net value to the recipient.

questions.q: Which organisation's primary role is to oversee and liberalise the rules of international trade between nations?
questions.explain: The World Trade Organization (WTO) governs the rules of world trade and adjudicates trade disputes.

questions.q: Anti-globalisation movements most commonly target which institutions?
options: The WTO, IMF and World Bank
questions.explain: Protesters often see the WTO, IMF and World Bank as promoting corporate-led, inequitable globalisation.

questions.q: Wallerstein's World Systems Theory describes superpowers as occupying the:
questions.explain: In World Systems Theory, dominant economies form the wealthy, exploitative 'core'.

questions.q: Hard power is best described as influence exerted through:
questions.explain: Hard power uses military strength and economic pressure such as sanctions or force to coerce others.

questions.q: The 'Asian Tigers' such as South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong became influential through:
questions.explain: The Asian Tigers grew rapidly via export-oriented manufacturing and investment in education.

questions.q: Which limitation most undermines GDP as a development measure?
options: It cannot be calculated for large economies
It says nothing about distribution, informal activity or wellbeing
questions.explain: GDP ignores income distribution, much informal activity and quality-of-life factors, so high GDP can mask deprivation.

questions.q: A criticism that TNCs avoid taxes by shifting profits between countries describes the problem of:
questions.explain: Transfer pricing lets TNCs book profits in low-tax jurisdictions, reducing tax paid in production countries.

questions.q: China's Belt and Road Initiative is best understood as a means of extending power through:
questions.explain: The Belt and Road Initiative builds infrastructure and trade links to expand China's economic and geopolitical influence.

questions.q: A criticism of an emerging multipolar world is that it may:
options: Create greater instability as power becomes more contested
questions.explain: With several competing powers, rivalry and miscalculation can make a multipolar order less stable.

questions.q: The 'legacy of empire' contributes to superpower status partly through:
options: Enduring language, institutional and trade ties such as the Commonwealth
questions.explain: Former empires often retain influence through shared language, legal systems and trade networks.

questions.q: How does poor health act as both a cause and consequence of underdevelopment?
options: Illness reduces productivity and incomes, while poverty limits access to healthcare
questions.explain: Disease lowers workforce productivity and earnings, and low incomes in turn restrict access to treatment, creating a cycle.

questions.q: Why is gender equality considered central to development?
options: It only matters in high-income countries
Empowering women raises education, health, productivity and reduces poverty
questions.explain: Educating and empowering women improves household welfare, child outcomes and economic growth, accelerating development.

questions.q: Fairtrade schemes aim to address inequalities in globalisation primarily by:
options: Guaranteeing producers a minimum price and a social premium
Removing all tariffs on luxury goods
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees minimum prices and a premium to give producers in poorer countries a fairer return.

questions.q: The G7 represents which group of states?
questions.explain: The G7 comprises leading advanced economies coordinating on global economic and political issues.

questions.q: The relocation of manufacturing from high-income to lower-income countries is best described as the:
questions.explain: The 'global shift' is the movement of manufacturing production to lower-cost economies, notably in Asia.

questions.q: What does the Gini coefficient measure?
options: Income or wealth inequality within a population
questions.explain: The Gini coefficient quantifies inequality, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality).

questions.q: The recent slowing of globalisation, with reduced growth in trade relative to GDP, has been nicknamed:
questions.explain: 'Slowbalisation' describes the post-2008 slowdown in the pace of global integration.

questions.q: A regional power is best defined as a state that:
options: Exerts strong influence within its own region but not globally
questions.explain: Regional powers, such as Brazil or South Africa, lead within their region but lack truly global reach.

questions.q: Reducing tariffs, quotas and other barriers to international trade is known as:
questions.explain: Trade liberalisation removes barriers to trade and has been a major driver of globalisation.

questions.q: Maintaining a network of overseas military bases gives a superpower:
options: Global military reach and the ability to project force
questions.explain: A worldwide base network lets a superpower deploy force rapidly across distant regions.

questions.q: The interdependence created by globalisation means that:
options: An economic shock in one country can rapidly spread to others
questions.explain: Interdependence means events such as the 2008 financial crisis transmit quickly through linked economies.

questions.q: How might trade rather than aid promote long-term development?
options: It builds sustainable income, industry and capacity within recipient economies
questions.explain: Fairer trade access can generate self-sustaining incomes and industrial capacity, unlike aid which can foster dependency.

questions.q: A world dominated by a single superpower is described as:
questions.explain: A unipolar world has one dominant power, as the USA was widely seen to be after 1991.

questions.q: Which best describes the shift in global power widely discussed since the 2000s?
options: From the West towards emerging Asian economies, especially China
From economic to purely military power
questions.explain: Many analysts describe an eastward shift of economic power towards China and emerging Asia.

questions.q: The global spread of US brands, films and universities is an example of which mechanism of power?
questions.explain: Cultural exports such as Hollywood and global brands extend US soft power and attractiveness.

questions.q: Possession of nuclear weapons contributes to superpower status mainly by providing:
options: A reliable source of energy exports
Strategic deterrence and global military leverage
questions.explain: Nuclear arsenals provide deterrence and reinforce a state's strategic, hard-power standing.

questions.q: Which institution primarily provides long-term loans and grants for development projects in poorer countries?
questions.explain: The World Bank funds long-term development projects such as infrastructure and poverty reduction.

questions.q: Intellectual property (IP) disputes between the USA and China are an example of:
questions.explain: Accusations of IP theft and forced technology transfer underpin economic and tech rivalry between the powers.
